scenes.caption: Risk is the summary a manager needs: how likely is this chain to run, and how bad is the impact if it does? The next figure shows how NIST turns those two answers into one level.

blocks.md: Here is the Mirai-style weakness in code, with its fix. The vulnerable version is short and works perfectly, which is why it shipped. The flaw is that the secret is the same on every device and printed in the manual, so it is not a secret.

blocks.code:
# VULNERABLE: every device of this model ships with the same login
DEFAULT_USER, DEFAULT_PASS = "admin", "admin"

def login(user, password):
    return user == DEFAULT_USER and password == DEFAULT_PASS
blocks.caption: Vulnerable: one shared factory login. Knowing the model number is enough to log in.

blocks.code:
# FIXED: no shared default; the owner must set a password on first boot
import hashlib, hmac, os

def set_password(password):
    if len(password) < 12:
        raise ValueError("choose at least 12 characters")
    salt = os.urandom(16)                     # random, different per device
    key = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
    return salt, key                          # store these, never the password

def check_password(password, salt, key):
    attempt = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
    return hmac.compare_digest(attempt, key)  # compare without timing leaks
blocks.caption: Fixed: each device gets its own password, stored only as a slow salted hash (scrypt), and compared in constant time.

blocks.md: Why the fix works: there is no longer any value an attacker can try on every device of the model. The password is chosen per device, so a list of 62 defaults finds nothing. Storing only a salted scrypt hash means a stolen settings file does not reveal the password, and `hmac.compare_digest` compares in a way that does not leak timing hints. The authentication course explains salts and slow hashes in depth. The **defender view**: you would spot a Mirai-style attack as many failed logins on ports 23 and 2323 in device or firewall logs (a firewall is a filter that allows or blocks network traffic by rule), and the fix is to disable Telnet and force a password change at setup.

**Risk** puts likelihood and impact together. NIST SP 800-30 (its guide to risk assessments) defines risk as a function of how likely a threat event is to happen and harm you, and how bad that harm would be. It gives a lookup table instead of a formula, so teams can rate both on a five-point scale and read off a risk level.

blocks.title: NIST SP 800-30 risk levels (Table I-2)

scenes.caption: Rows are likelihood, columns are impact. Cell values are the risk level: 0 very low, 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high, 4 very high (copied from the table).
An internet-facing camera with a default password, while botnets scan for it all day: very high likelihood. The impact to its owner is moderate, so the risk is moderate (2).
A flaw in a hospital system, low likelihood but very high impact: still moderate (2). Rare but severe events are not automatically low risk.
Likelihood matters as much as impact: at high impact, very high likelihood gives high (3) but moderate likelihood only moderate (2). NIST says organisations may tailor the table.

blocks.md: A vulnerability is not a risk by itself. A severe bug in software you do not run, or on a machine with no network connection, may carry very little risk. A boring weakness on an internet-facing system that attackers already scan for can carry a lot. Lesson 6 turns this into a patching order.

Vulnerability = the weakness. Threat = who or what could use it. Exploit = the act or code that uses it. Payload = what runs afterwards. Risk = likelihood times impact. You remove risk by fixing vulnerabilities, reducing exposure, or reducing impact (backups, segmentation).

blocks.question: A researcher publishes code that shows a router bug can be triggered, but nobody has used it against anyone. Which word fits that code best?
options: A threat source
A payload already in the wild
A risk
A proof-of-concept exploit
blocks.explain: Code that demonstrates a vulnerability can be exploited is a proof of concept (PoC). It is not yet active exploitation: CISA says PoC code and security research do not count as exploitation in the wild. The threat source is a person or group, and risk is an assessment, not code.

blocks.question: Using the NIST table, which change lowers the risk of the internet-facing camera the most?
options: Make the camera's case tamper-proof
Remove the default password and turn Telnet off
Write a policy that says cameras must be secure
Move the camera to a different room
blocks.explain: Removing the vulnerability that botnets scan for drops the likelihood from very high to low, which moves the cell from moderate to low. The other options do not touch the path the attack actually uses.

lessons.title: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors

blocks.md:
Every way an attacker can interact with a system is a possible way in. NIST SP 800-53 calls the set of those points the **attack surface**: the points on a system's boundary where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect, or extract data.

Tiny example: your laptop. Its attack surface includes every program listening on the network, every file or link you open, every USB port, and you, the person who types the password. A service you never use but left running is still a door. A smaller attack surface means fewer doors to guard.

Defenders start by listing their own doors. On Linux, the `ss` tool (socket statistics) shows which programs are waiting for network connections over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol, the standard way programs open connections on the internet). `0.0.0.0` means "listening on every network interface", so anyone who can reach the machine can knock. `127.0.0.1` is the loopback address: only programs on the same machine can connect.

blocks.code:
$ ss -tlnp        # t: TCP, l: listening, n: numeric, p: owning process
State   Recv-Q Send-Q  Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port  Process
LISTEN  0      128           0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*      users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3))
LISTEN  0      511           0.0.0.0:80         0.0.0.0:*      users:(("nginx",pid=930,fd=6))
LISTEN  0      244         127.0.0.1:5432       0.0.0.0:*      users:(("postgres",pid=701,fd=5))
blocks.caption: Illustrative output on your own server. SSH (Secure Shell, encrypted remote login, port 22) and the web server (80) are reachable from the network; the PostgreSQL database (5432) only from this machine.

blocks.md:
Each line is a decision. If nobody uses SSH from outside, close it or restrict it to an administrators' network. If the database must stay local, keep it bound to 127.0.0.1. Reducing attack surface is often the cheapest security work there is, because a closed door needs no patching.

Now a case that made the idea famous. On 2 November 1988 a program spread across the young internet, infecting hundreds or thousands of computers and making many of them unusable (Donn Seeley, a University of Utah computer scientist, in the analysis below). A US federal appeals court later summarised it: Robert Tappan Morris, then a first-year computer science PhD student at Cornell University, wrote a **worm** and released it from a computer at MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) to hide where it came from. RFC 1135 (an RFC, Request for Comments, is an internet community document) defines a worm as a program that runs on its own and copies a complete working version of itself to other machines, unlike a virus, which needs a host program to run.

blocks.title: The four doors the Morris worm used

scenes.caption: The court listed four ways in. Each is a different kind of attack surface: two network services with bugs, a trust feature, and people's password choices.
Door 1: sendmail, the program that delivered email, had a non-standard debug command (RFC 1135). The worm used it to send itself to the remote machine and start running there.
Door 2: fingerd answered questions about users. It read requests with gets() into a 512-byte buffer without checking length; the worm sent a longer one (next figure).
Door 3: trusted-hosts files let a user on one machine log in to another without a password. Once on one machine, the worm followed that trust to its neighbours.
Door 4: password guessing. RFC 1135 says it tried no password, the user name (also doubled), the nickname, the last name (also reversed), a built-in list of 432 words, and the system dictionary.
Then it copied itself onward. To resist fake 'already infected' answers, it reinfected anyway one time in seven; that ratio made machines run many copies and grind to a halt.

blocks.md: Door 2 is the first famous **buffer overflow**: a program writes more data into a fixed-size area of memory (a buffer) than it can hold, and the extra bytes overwrite whatever sits next to it. Donn Seeley's analysis, *A Tour of the Worm*, explains that fingerd read the request with the C library function `gets()`, which does not check the 512-byte buffer's size. The worm's 536-byte request overwrote the saved address the program would jump back to when the function finished, so the program jumped into the worm's own code. The memory safety course shows this byte by byte; here is the shape of it.

blocks.title: A fixed buffer and the value stored after it (simplified)

scenes.caption: Simplified: six cells stand for fingerd's 512-byte buffer, and RET for the saved return address that tells the program where to continue when the function ends.
A normal request (a user name) fits. The rest of the buffer is unused and RET is untouched.
gets() keeps copying until it sees a newline. A longer request fills the buffer and spills into RET, so the attacker now decides where the program goes next.
fgets() is told the buffer size. It stops one cell early, adds the terminator, and RET survives. Extra input is simply left unread.

blocks.caption: The bug and the fix in C. gets() cannot know the buffer size; fgets() is given it. gets() was later deprecated and then removed from the C standard in C11.

blocks.md: The **defender response** in 1988 is listed in RFC 1135: isolate machines from the network, turn off mail service or patch out the sendmail debug command, shut down or fix fingerd, and require new passwords for every user. Every item maps to one door. The legal ending matters too: Morris was convicted under the then-new US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and sentenced to three years of probation, 400 hours of community service and a USD 10,050 fine (lesson 12 returns to this law). The court accepted that the goal had been to demonstrate weak security; it still counted as access without authorisation.

blocks.prompt: The worm checked whether a machine was already infected before copying itself. Why did the machines still drown in copies?
blocks.reveal: Because Morris worried that administrators could fake the "already infected" answer, the worm copied itself anyway one time in seven, as the court opinion records. Morris underestimated how often each machine would be asked, so the 1-in-7 rule produced far more copies than intended, and machines slowed to a halt. The damage came as much from **availability** loss (CPU and disk exhausted) as from the break-in itself.

blocks.md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

blocks.question: Your web server also runs a database that only the web app on the same machine uses. Which `ss` line would worry you?
options: LISTEN on 0.0.0.0:80
LISTEN on 0.0.0.0:5432
No line for port 5432 at all
blocks.explain: 0.0.0.0 means the database accepts connections from any network the machine is on, which adds a door nobody needs. 127.0.0.1 keeps it local. Port 80 is the web server, which is meant to be reachable.

blocks.question: Which Morris worm door involved no programming bug at all?
options: Trusted-hosts logins and guessable passwords
fingerd reading input with gets()
sendmail's debug command
None: every door was a coding error
blocks.explain: Trusted hosts worked exactly as designed, and weak passwords are a human choice. Attack surface includes features and people, not just bugs. The fingerd and sendmail doors were implementation errors.

lessons.title: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists

blocks.md:
Knowing who might attack tells you what they want, how hard they will try and what they will do once inside. NIST SP 800-30 sorts **threat sources** into four types:

- **Adversarial**: individuals, groups, organisations or nation states that deliberately try to harm you. NIST describes them by *capability* (skill and resources), *intent* (what they want) and *targeting* (whether they picked you).
- **Accidental**: mistakes by ordinary users or administrators.
- **Structural**: failing hardware, software or environmental controls.
- **Environmental**: fires, floods, power and network outages.

Security people spend most of their time on the first type, but the other three cause plenty of outages, and the same backups protect against all of them.

The adversaries you will meet most often:

- **Cybercriminals** want money: card fraud, stolen data to sell, or access to sell to other criminals.
- **Ransomware groups** are criminals who encrypt victims' data and demand payment (**ransomware** is malicious software that encrypts files so they and the systems that rely on them are unusable, per CISA). Many run as **ransomware-as-a-service** (RaaS): CISA explains that developers write the ransomware and take a share of the proceeds from **affiliates**, the criminals who break in and deploy it. Many also practise **double extortion**: steal data first, then demand a second payment to not publish it.
- **Nation states** want intelligence, influence, sabotage and sometimes money. They have the most resources and patience.
- **Insiders** are people with legitimate access. NIST's definition notes they may cause harm *wittingly or unwittingly*: selling data and emailing it to the wrong person both count.
- **Hacktivists** attack to promote a political or social cause, usually seeking publicity.

blocks.title: Adversaries and what they usually want

scenes.caption: Motive predicts behaviour. Money-driven attackers pick targets that can pay and move fast; spies stay hidden for as long as possible.
Ransomware: Colonial Pipeline, 2021 (below). The group DarkSide said publicly it preferred targets that can afford large ransoms, according to CISA.
States sometimes chase money too. The UK National Cyber Security Centre assessed it highly likely that North Korean actors, the Lazarus Group, were behind WannaCry (lesson 7).
Insiders already hold valid access, so perimeter defences do not see them. Logging who reads what, and giving people only the access they need, are the counters.

blocks.md: **Case: Colonial Pipeline, May 2021.** Colonial runs a fuel pipeline of more than 5,500 miles that, in its chief executive Joseph Blount's words to the US Senate, carries nearly half the fuel consumed on the US East Coast. Blount testified that the company was hit by the criminal group DarkSide, which encrypted its **IT** (information technology: office and business) systems. Two terms you need: a **VPN** (virtual private network) is an encrypted tunnel that lets remote users reach an internal network; **OT** (operational technology) is the network of computers that physically control the pipeline.

blocks.title: Colonial Pipeline, 7 May 2021, as testified

scenes.caption: Blount: the attacker used a legacy VPN profile not meant to be in use; how it got the credentials was still unknown. Mandiant, the response firm, told Bloomberg the break-in was on 29 April, 8 days before the note.
DarkSide ransomware encrypted IT systems. CISA's advisory says DarkSide actors encrypt and steal data, then threaten to publish it.
Just before 5:00 AM an employee found the ransom note. The control centre ordered a stop to keep the malware from spreading into OT, which may or may not have been reached.
Shutdown began about 5:55 AM; by 6:10 AM all 5,500 miles were stopped. The OT network was not shown to be encrypted: the shutdown was a precaution.

Colonial contacted the FBI and CISA, paid about 75 bitcoins in ransom (Blount called it one of the toughest decisions of their life) and restarted from the evening of 12 May. In June the FBI seized back 63.7 bitcoins.

blocks.md: Notice what the attacker did *not* need: no new bug, no exploit code. An old remote-access account that nobody used was still switched on, and someone had its password. That is attack surface (lesson 3) owned by nobody. A defender can hunt for exactly this with a short script over an account export. The script below flags enabled accounts that have never logged in or have been idle for 90 days, which are the ones to disable or review.

blocks.code:
import csv
from datetime import date, datetime

STALE_DAYS = 90
today = date.today()

# export from the VPN or identity system; columns: user,enabled,last_login
with open("vpn_accounts.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        if row["enabled"] != "yes":
            continue
        if not row["last_login"]:
            print("NEVER USED but enabled:", row["user"])
            continue
        last = datetime.strptime(row["last_login"], "%Y-%m-%d").date()
        if (today - last).days > STALE_DAYS:
            print("STALE:", row["user"], "last login", last)
blocks.caption: Defender view: find enabled remote-access accounts nobody is using. Columns and file name are illustrative; real exports differ by product.

blocks.md: Detection signals for this kind of entry: a login to a dormant account, a VPN login from an unusual country or at an unusual hour, and a new device for an existing user. Most VPN and identity products log these; someone has to read the log or alert on it.

Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access. Insiders already have access. The defence emphasis differs for each, but removing unused access helps against all of them.

blocks.question: A company's main worry is ransomware affiliates. Which control best reduces that specific threat?
options: A bigger firewall rule set for outbound web traffic only
Hiding the company's logo from its website
Encrypting the data at rest on servers
Offline backups plus removing unused remote-access accounts
blocks.explain: Affiliates commonly enter through exposed remote access with stolen credentials and profit by making data unavailable. Removing unused access shrinks their entry points, and offline backups (which CISA's DarkSide advisory recommends) remove the leverage. Encryption at rest does not stop ransomware from encrypting the data again.

blocks.question: An employee accidentally shares a folder of customer records publicly. In NIST's taxonomy, this threat source is:
options: Adversarial: nation state
Accidental: a user's error
Structural: hardware failure
Environmental: infrastructure outage
blocks.explain: NIST classes erroneous actions by people doing their everyday work as accidental threat sources. The harm (a confidentiality loss) is real even with no attacker.

lessons.title: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD

blocks.md:
A vulnerability has a life story. Someone writes buggy code. Later, someone finds the bug: the vendor's own engineers, an outside researcher, or an attacker. What happens next decides how dangerous it is.

Tiny example: a researcher notices that a router's login page crashes on very long passwords. They can tell the vendor privately, publish it immediately, sell it, or use it. Security has words and institutions for each of these paths.

- A **zero-day** is a vulnerability that attackers exploit while it is still unknown to the vendor and the public. The US national security glossary (CNSSI 4009) defines a zero-day attack as one that exploits a previously unknown hardware, firmware or software vulnerability. The defenders have had zero days to fix it.
- **Coordinated vulnerability disclosure** (CVD; older name *responsible disclosure*): the finder reports privately, the vendor builds a fix, and details are published together with the fix. CISA runs a CVD program to coordinate this when many vendors are involved.
- **Deadline-based disclosure**: Google's Project Zero, a team that hunts bugs in widely used software, gives vendors a fixed window (90 days under its [current policy](https://googleprojectzero.blogspot.com/p/vulnerability-disclosure-policy.html), with plans announced to shorten it) and publishes after it, fixed or not; if a bug is already being exploited in the wild, the window is 7 days.
- **Full disclosure**: publishing everything at once, with no fix ready. It pressures vendors but arms attackers first.

Once a bug is public, people need one shared name for it. That is the **CVE** system (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). CISA explains it: a CVE ID is a unique identifier for a publicly known vulnerability; the CVE Program is sponsored by CISA and run by The MITRE Corporation, a US non-profit that operates federally funded research centres. IDs are assigned by a **CNA** (CVE Numbering Authority): an organisation authorised to number bugs within its own scope, such as a software vendor, open-source project, coordination centre or bug bounty platform. A CVE record is *Reserved* when the ID is set aside, *Published* once it has a description and at least one public reference, or *Rejected* if it should not be used.

An ID looks like `CVE-2017-0144`: the prefix, a year, and a sequence number. The digits say nothing about severity.

blocks.title: From private report to public record (coordinated disclosure)

scenes.caption: The finder reports privately, usually to a security contact the vendor publishes (lesson 12 shows the security.txt file for this).
Big vendors are their own CNA. Microsoft reserved CVE-2017-0144 on 9 Sep 2016, months before the bug was public, so the year in an ID is not a disclosure date.
Fix and advisory ship together. For CVE-2017-0144 the fix was bulletin MS17-010 on 14 Mar 2017; the CVE record was published on 17 Mar.
NIST's National Vulnerability Database mirrors every CVE and adds analysis: a CVSS severity score, affected product names and a weakness type.
Now the race begins: defenders must patch before attackers turn the advisory into working attacks. Lessons 7 and 8 show what happens when they lose it.

blocks.md:
The **NVD** (National Vulnerability Database) is maintained by NIST. CISA's description: it is synchronised with the CVE List and adds impact metrics, product names and other analysis. Two of those additions you will see everywhere: **CVSS**, a severity score from 0 to 10 (next lesson), and **CWE** (Common Weakness Enumeration), a catalogue of bug types such as CWE-755, improper handling of exceptional conditions, which NVD assigns to the Struts bug behind the Equifax breach.

The NVD has a public API (application programming interface: a way for programs to ask for data). This is a defender's first move when a CVE ID appears in the news.

blocks.code:
# Ask the NVD API for one CVE and keep the fields a defender reads first
curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2017-5638" \
  | jq '.vulnerabilities[0].cve | {id, published,
        score: .metrics.cvssMetricV31[0].cvssData.baseScore,
        kev_added: .cisaExploitAdd}'

# output when this course was written
{
  "id": "CVE-2017-5638",
  "published": "2017-03-11T02:59:00.150",
  "score": 9.8,
  "kev_added": "2021-11-03"
}
blocks.caption: Look up a CVE from the command line. jq (a JSON query tool) picks the fields. kev_added says when CISA listed it as exploited in the wild (next lesson).

blocks.prompt: A vendor learns of a bug from a researcher on day 0 and ships a fix on day 47. Under a 90-day deadline policy like Project Zero's, when are the details published?
blocks.reveal: **On day 90**, not day 47. Project Zero's policy uses a fixed window: details are published at the end of it whether the fix came early or not at all, which gives users time to install the patch before the full technical details are out. If the bug were already being exploited in the wild, the window would be 7 days instead.

blocks.md: "Zero-day" describes the defenders' situation (no fix existed), not how clever the attack is. Most real breaches use **known** vulnerabilities with patches available for weeks or years. Equifax (lesson 8) is the textbook example.

Path of a vulnerability: found, reported, fixed, numbered (CVE via a CNA), published with a patch, enriched by NVD (CVSS, CWE, products), patched by users. Attackers can enter at any point; the gap between patch release and patch install is where most damage happens.

blocks.question: Why does the security world need CVE IDs at all?
options: They give every publicly known vulnerability one shared name that scanners, advisories and people can refer to
They encrypt vulnerability details so attackers cannot read them
They rate how dangerous a bug is
They prove the vendor has fixed the bug
blocks.explain: A CVE ID is an identifier, nothing more. Severity is CVSS's job, exploitation status is KEV's, and fix status comes from the vendor advisory. One name lets a scanner report, a vendor bulletin and a news story be matched up.

blocks.question: Attackers exploit a flaw in a VPN appliance before the vendor knows it exists. What is this called?
options: Coordinated disclosure
A CNA
A zero-day attack
An n-day patch
blocks.explain: An attack on a previously unknown vulnerability is a zero-day attack: the vendor has had zero days to produce a fix. Coordinated disclosure is the opposite path, where the vendor hears first.

lessons.title: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS

blocks.md:
A large company may have thousands of unpatched CVEs at any moment. It cannot fix them all today, so it needs an order. Three public tools help, and they answer different questions:

- **CVSS**: how severe is this bug in general?
- **KEV**: is anyone actually exploiting it?
- **EPSS**: how likely is it to be exploited soon?

**CVSS** (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is owned by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), a non-profit for incident response teams. Its **base score** describes a vulnerability's built-in characteristics on a 0 to 10 scale, and is written with a **vector string** that records every input, for example `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`.

Read that vector left to right. Exploitability metrics: **AV** attack vector (N network, A adjacent network, L local, P physical), **AC** attack complexity (L low, H high), **PR** privileges the attacker needs first (N none, L low, H high), **UI** user interaction (N none, R required), **S** scope (U unchanged: the damage stays in the vulnerable component; C changed: it reaches others). Impact metrics: **C**, **I**, **A**, the CIA triad from lesson 1, each H high, L low or N none.

The CVSS v3.1 specification turns them into numbers with fixed constants (network 0.85, low complexity 0.77, high impact 0.56, and so on) and these formulas, for scope unchanged:

blocks.caption: ISS is the impact sub-score. Scope-changed bugs use a different impact formula and a 1.08 multiplier.
Roundup rounds up to one decimal place (4.02 becomes 4.1). The spec's appendix gives an integer method to avoid floating-point surprises.

blocks.title: Computing the base score of CVE-2017-5638 (Equifax's Struts bug)

vars.v: AV:N AC:L PR:N UI:N S:U C:H I:H A:H

scenes.caption: NVD's v3.1 vector for the Apache Struts bug: reachable over the network, easy, no account, no user click, full impact on all three properties.
The vector is split into a dictionary of metric to value.
1 minus (1 - 0.56) cubed = 1 - 0.0852 = 0.9148. Three high impacts compound, but ISS can never exceed 1.
Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85. Every 'easiest' choice at once gives the maximum, 3.887.
The sum is 9.7602, below the cap of 10. Roundup lifts it to the next tenth.
9.8: Critical (the spec's bands are Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9, Critical 9.0 to 10.0). This matches NVD's published score.

blocks.title: How single metrics move the base score (computed with the code above)

scenes.caption: All five keep C:H/I:H/A:H and UI:N, so only exploitability changes. The Struts vector scores 9.8.
NVD scores the EternalBlue bug, CVE-2017-0144, as needing low privileges (8.8). Microsoft's bulletin says an unauthenticated attacker could exploit it, and WannaCry did. Vectors are judgement calls.
Needing physical access drops the same impact to 6.8, Medium. Distance from the attacker matters as much as the damage.

blocks.md:
The specification itself warns that the base score is a severity, not your risk: it assumes the reasonable worst case, and consumers should add their own context, such as how many customers depend on the system. The newer **CVSS v4.0** has four metric groups (Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental), where v3.1 had Base, Temporal and Environmental, and FIRST notes that databases such as NVD typically publish only the base score.

**KEV** (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) is a catalogue run by CISA, created by Binding Operational Directive 22-01 on 3 November 2021 (a binding operational directive is an order US federal agencies must follow). An entry needs three things: a CVE ID, reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild, and a clear fix. CISA explained the reason in 22-01: by its study, fewer than 4% of all CVEs had been exploited in the wild, so patching the exploited ones first gives the most protection per hour. A 2026 directive, BOD 26-04, now sets the federal deadlines and carries the KEV criteria forward.

**EPSS** (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), also from FIRST, is a machine-learning model that estimates the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, recalculated daily for every CVE. When this course was written, both CVEs above had EPSS above 0.99: they are old, famous and still attacked.

A sensible order for a beginner's patch queue: KEV entries on internet-facing systems first, then high-EPSS and critical-CVSS bugs on exposed systems, then the rest by CVSS and asset value.

blocks.prompt: Bug A: CVSS 9.1, on an internal test server, not in KEV, EPSS 0.01. Bug B: CVSS 7.5, on your public login portal, listed in KEV. Which do you patch first?
blocks.reveal: **Bug B.** It is being exploited by real attackers right now (KEV), and it sits on your most exposed system. Bug A is more severe on paper, but nobody is known to use it and it is hard to reach. CISA's reasoning for KEV is exactly this: a small share of vulnerabilities cause most of the harm, so exploitation evidence beats raw severity. Patch A soon too; "later" is not "never".

blocks.md: CVSS = how bad in theory. KEV = being used now. EPSS = likely to be used soon. Combine them with what *your* asset is and how exposed it is. A score without context is not a priority.

blocks.question: A vector changes from UI:N to UI:R (a user must click something). With everything else the same, what happens to the base score?
options: It goes up, because users are unreliable
It stays the same, because UI is an impact metric
It drops to 0
It goes down, because the exploitability term shrinks (0.85 becomes 0.62)
blocks.explain: UI is an exploitability metric. Required interaction makes the attack harder, so the multiplier falls from 0.85 to 0.62 and the base score drops. Impact is unchanged.

blocks.question: Which statement about KEV is correct?
options: Every critical CVSS bug is in KEV
A KEV entry needs a CVE ID, reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild, and a clear remediation
A public proof-of-concept is required for KEV
KEV replaces CVSS scores in the NVD
blocks.explain: These are CISA's three criteria. CISA says a public PoC is not required, many critical bugs are never exploited and so never listed, and NVD still publishes CVSS scores alongside the KEV date.

lessons.title: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm

blocks.md:
This case shows the whole vulnerability life cycle in one spring, and why "a patch exists" is not the end of the story.

Some vocabulary first. **SMB** (Server Message Block) is the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing; it is reached over TCP port 445. **SMBv1** is its oldest version. The **NSA** is the US National Security Agency. **EternalBlue** is the name of a leaked exploit for a bug in Windows' SMBv1 server, tracked as CVE-2017-0144. Microsoft's description: an attacker could send a specially crafted packet to an SMBv1 server and run code on it, in most cases without authenticating.

blocks.title: Spring 2017, in days after the patch

scenes.caption: Day 0 (14 Mar 2017): Microsoft publishes bulletin MS17-010, rated Critical, fixing several SMBv1 bugs in supported Windows versions.

Day 31 (14 Apr): a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers dumps tools it says were stolen from the NSA, including EternalBlue. Ars Technica's update: none were zero-days against supported, patched Windows.
Many organisations have still not patched. Every day of this window, a free, working exploit is public.
Day 59 (12 May): WannaCry ransomware spreads by itself using EternalBlue. CISA cited reports of tens of thousands of infections in over 150 countries, spreading over several hours.
Day 60 (13 May): Microsoft also releases fixes for Windows XP, Windows 8 and Server 2003 (per CISA), versions the March bulletin, written for supported releases, had not covered.

blocks.md:
WannaCry was **ransomware that behaved like a worm**. CISA's analysis: once running, it installed itself as a Windows service, scanned the local network for machines answering on SMB ports, and used the MS17-010 vulnerability to copy itself to each one it could reach. No one had to click anything on the second machine. That is what **wormable** means: a bug that lets malicious code spread from machine to machine with no human help.

It also carried a **kill switch**. CISA: before doing anything, it tried to reach a long, unregistered web domain; if the connection succeeded, it quit. UK researcher Marcus Hutchins, writing as MalwareTech, registered that domain to track infections, as [Hutchins' own write-up](https://www.malwaretech.com/2017/05/how-to-accidentally-stop-a-global-cyber-attacks.html) explains, and doing so stopped new infections from encrypting. The National Audit Office says the attack would have caused more disruption without that.

blocks.title: Why patching and SMBv1 settings decided who was hit

scenes.caption: One infected machine scans its neighbours over SMB. What happens next depends only on each neighbour's state, not on anyone's behaviour.
The unpatched PC is taken over and becomes a scanner itself, reaching the unpatched server. Spread is exponential inside flat networks.
The patched PC receives the same packets and nothing happens. A machine with SMBv1 removed has no vulnerable code to reach at all.
Once the kill-switch domain answered, newly started copies exited before encrypting. Machines already encrypted stayed encrypted: the switch did not undo damage.

blocks.md:
**The NHS.** The UK National Audit Office (NAO) found at least 81 of the 236 hospital trusts in England were affected, plus 603 primary care and other NHS organisations, including 595 GP practices. NHS England identified 6,912 cancelled appointments and estimated over 19,000 in total. Its blunt conclusion: infected organisations had unpatched or unsupported Windows, NHS Digital had issued critical alerts to patch in March and April 2017, and it was a relatively unsophisticated attack that basic IT security practice could have prevented.

**Who did it.** The UK National Cyber Security Centre assessed it highly likely that North Korean actors known as the Lazarus Group were behind WannaCry, and the US government made the same public attribution.

**Defender view.** CISA's guidance was, in order: apply MS17-010; if you cannot, disable SMBv1 and block SMB at the network boundary (TCP 445, plus TCP 139 and UDP 137 to 138); keep tested backups; segment networks. Detection signals: one workstation suddenly opening many connections on port 445, and a new service appearing (CISA names WannaCry's, `mssecsvc2.0`). Microsoft's documentation shows how to check for and remove SMBv1 safely.

blocks.code:
# Run in an elevated PowerShell on Windows (from Microsoft's SMB guidance)

# 1. Is the SMBv1 server enabled?
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select EnableSMB1Protocol

# 2. Find who still uses it before you remove it: logs Event ID 3000 in
#    Microsoft-Windows-SMBServer/Audit for every SMBv1 connection attempt
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -AuditSmb1Access $true

# 3. Remove the SMBv1 feature entirely
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol
blocks.caption: From Microsoft's guide to detecting and disabling SMBv1. Audit first so you learn which old devices still need it, then remove the feature.

blocks.prompt: A hospital patched every Windows machine on 20 March 2017 but left SMBv1 enabled. Is it safe from WannaCry's EternalBlue spreading?
blocks.reveal: **From EternalBlue spreading, yes.** MS17-010 fixed the vulnerable code, so the same packets do nothing. SMBv1 being enabled is still worth removing (it is old, and other bugs may follow), but WannaCry's network spread depended on the unpatched bug. CISA treated disabling SMBv1 and blocking port 445 as the fallbacks for organisations that *could not* patch.

blocks.md: The leak did not create the vulnerability; it created a free, reliable exploit. The patch already existed for 59 days. Treat every critical advisory as if working exploit code will be public soon, because sometimes it already is.

WannaCry: one wormable bug, a patch two months old, a leaked exploit, and organisations that had not patched or could not patch old systems. The fixes were basic: patch, remove legacy protocols, filter port 445, segment, back up.

blocks.question: What made WannaCry spread so much faster than ordinary ransomware sent by email?
options: It used a zero-day that no patch could fix
It encrypted files faster
It exploited a network service directly, so each infected machine infected others with no user action
It targeted only hospitals
blocks.explain: The SMBv1 bug was reachable over the network without authentication, so WannaCry behaved like a worm. MS17-010 had already fixed it, so it was not a zero-day for patched systems.

blocks.question: An organisation cannot patch an old Windows Server this week. Which CISA fallback reduces the risk most?
options: Disable SMBv1 and block SMB ports at the network boundary
Turn off Windows Update
Rename the server
Pay for a larger internet connection
blocks.explain: CISA recommended disabling SMBv1 and blocking TCP 445 and related ports at the boundary when the patch could not be applied. This removes or hides the vulnerable code path.

lessons.title: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch

blocks.md:
Equifax is a consumer credit reporting agency: it collects data about people's borrowing and sells credit reports. In 2017 attackers stole personal data on 148 million people, which the US House Oversight Committee's report calls nearly half the US population. The committee's verdict: the breach was entirely preventable. In 2020 the US Department of Justice charged four members of China's People's Liberation Army (PLA), its military, with the intrusion; charges are allegations, not proof.

The bug was in **Apache Struts**, an open-source framework (ready-made building blocks) for writing Java web applications. CVE-2017-5638, in NVD's words: the Jakarta Multipart parser in Struts 2.3.x before 2.3.32 and 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 mishandles errors during file uploads, which lets remote attackers run arbitrary commands through a crafted `Content-Type` HTTP header (HTTP, Hypertext Transfer Protocol, is how browsers and web servers talk) (the header that tells a server what kind of data a request carries). Apache's advisory, S2-045, rated it Critical and said: upgrade.

blocks.title: Equifax 2017, in days after Apache's fix (House Oversight report)

scenes.caption: Day 0 (7 Mar): Apache discloses CVE-2017-5638 and releases fixed versions. Day 1: US-CERT (the US Computer Emergency Readiness Team) alerts Equifax.

Day 2: Equifax's vulnerability team emails over 400 people asking anyone running Struts to patch within 48 hours. Day 3: first evidence of attackers exploiting the bug on servers connected to Equifax's network.

Day 8: a scan for the vulnerability finds nothing on external systems. But ACIS (Automated Consumer Interview System), a dispute portal from the 1970s, still ran vulnerable Struts. Nobody had it on a list.
Day 67 (13 May): attackers enter through ACIS and install web shells (web pages that act as a remote control). They find a file of unencrypted passwords and query 48 databases about 9,000 times.
The device that inspected ACIS traffic had been blind for 19 months because its security certificate had expired. Day 144 (29 Jul): the certificate is renewed and suspicious traffic is seen at once.
Day 145: ACIS is taken offline, ending the attack. Day 184 (7 Sep): Equifax announces the breach, first counting 143 million people, later 148 million.

blocks.md:
The patch existed for 67 days before the break-in. So why did it fail? The committee's answer is the most important lesson in vulnerability management: **you cannot patch what you do not know you run.** Equifax's patch policy relied on each system owner knowing the software and versions inside their applications. The executive responsible for ACIS told investigators that, when the breach was announced, they had not even been aware that Struts ran in that environment. Witnesses described separate inventory lists kept by different teams.

Then each later layer failed too: the scan missed the system, the monitoring device was silently off for 19 months, passwords sat unencrypted in a file, and one compromised application could reach 48 unrelated databases.

An **asset inventory** (a list of every system and the software and versions it runs) turns an advisory into a to-do list. The script below is the core of what a software inventory tool does with an advisory like S2-045: compare every recorded version against the first fixed version for its branch. The application names are made up.

blocks.title: Turning an advisory into a patch list

scenes.caption: From the advisory: each release branch has a first fixed version. Versions are compared as tuples of numbers, not as text (as text, 2.3.4 would sort after 2.3.32).
careers-site runs exactly the fixed version.
Not vulnerable.
dispute-portal is one release behind on the 2.3 branch: vulnerable. In 2017, this is the line that never printed for ACIS, because ACIS was not in the inventory.

scenes.output:
careers-site 2.5.10.1 False
dispute-portal 2.3.31 True
intranet 2.5.8 True
scenes.caption: intranet is behind on the 2.5 branch: vulnerable too. Internal systems still need the patch, because attackers who get in anywhere can reach them.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevent: a single, automatically built inventory of software and versions (later courses call it an SBOM, software bill of materials), patch deadlines tracked to completion rather than by email, and network segmentation so one application cannot reach 48 databases. Detect: outbound traffic inspection that alerts when it stops working (an expired certificate should be a page to someone, not a silent failure), and alerts on large or unusual database queries. Respond: the moment the monitor worked again, Equifax noticed the suspicious traffic immediately.

blocks.prompt: Equifax's 15 March scan found no vulnerable external systems. Give two reasons a scan can miss a vulnerable application.
blocks.reveal:
Any two of these:
1. **It never scanned that system**, because the target list came from an incomplete inventory.
2. **The scanner could not see the version**: an application can bundle a library deep inside it, and a scan from outside may not reach the code path that reveals it.
3. **The scan was misconfigured** or checked the wrong ports or URLs.

For Equifax the House report names one cause: Equifax's interim security chief said an open-source component scan missed Struts because it was run on the root directory, not the subdirectory where Struts was listed (reason 3). The general lesson: a clean scan is evidence, not proof. Pair scans with an inventory built from the systems themselves.

blocks.md: Equifax failed at the boring basics: inventory, patch tracking, credential storage, segmentation and monitoring health. No single failure caused the breach; every layer had a hole, which is the subject of lesson 10.

blocks.question: Struts 2.5.10 is installed. Is it vulnerable to CVE-2017-5638?
options: No: 2.5.10 is newer than 2.3.32
No: only 2.3.x was affected
It depends on the CVSS score
Yes: on the 2.5 branch the first fixed version is 2.5.10.1
blocks.explain: NVD lists 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 as affected. Comparing across branches (2.5.10 against 2.3.32) is the classic mistake; compare within the branch.

blocks.question: Which single fix would have let Equifax see the attack months earlier?
options: A longer password policy
Keeping the traffic-inspection device's certificate valid, with an alert when it is not
Changing the dispute portal's colour scheme
Encrypting the database backups
blocks.explain: The House report says suspicious traffic was noticed immediately after the expired certificate was renewed on 29 July. The monitoring device had been blind for 19 months.

lessons.title: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK

blocks.md:
Attacks are not one event. Before Equifax's data left the building, attackers had to find a weak system, break in, keep access, find passwords, search databases and move data out. Each step is a chance for defenders to notice or stop them. Two models give those steps names.

Eric Hutchins, Michael Cloppert and Rohan Amin of Lockheed Martin, a US defence contractor, published the **intrusion kill chain**. They borrowed the term from military targeting doctrine, where a kill chain is the sequence find, fix, track, target, engage, assess; it is called a chain because any one broken link interrupts the whole process. Their seven phases for computer intrusions follow.

blocks.title: Lockheed Martin's intrusion kill chain

scenes.caption: Seven phases, as defined in the paper. The attacker must complete every one; the defender needs to stop only one.
Reconnaissance: research and pick targets, for example by crawling websites for email addresses. Weaponization: couple an exploit with a remote-access program into a deliverable payload.
Delivery: get the payload to the target (the paper's most common vectors were email attachments, websites and USB drives). Exploitation: trigger the attacker's code, usually through a vulnerability.
Installation: a backdoor gives persistence. Command and control (C2): the victim machine calls out to the attacker's server, giving hands-on-keyboard access.
Actions on objectives: only now does the attacker reach the goal, typically stealing data, or harming integrity or availability.
Equifax on the chain: the Struts bug (exploit), web shells (install), 76 days of access (C2) and 9,000 queries (actions). Monitoring could have cut it at C2; patching at exploit.

blocks.md:
The paper's key claim, in its words: in a kill chain model, just one mitigation breaks the chain and thwarts the adversary. Defenders should plan a detection or block for every phase, not only the first.

The kill chain is good for strategy but coarse. **MITRE ATT&CK** (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is the detailed version. MITRE started it in 2013 to document how real attackers behave inside Windows enterprise networks, and it now covers cloud, mobile and industrial systems. It has two key ideas:

- A **tactic** is the attacker's goal at a step, the *why*: Initial Access, Persistence, Credential Access, Lateral Movement (moving from one machine to the next), Exfiltration (moving data out), Impact, and so on. The current Enterprise matrix lists 15 tactics; the list is revised between versions.
- A **technique** is *how* they achieve it, with a stable ID: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact.

blocks.code:
# Equifax 2017 mapped to ATT&CK (a simplified reading of the House report)
- step: Exploited Apache Struts on the ACIS portal
  tactic: Initial Access
  technique: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application
- step: Installed web shells to keep remote control
  tactic: Persistence
  technique: T1505.003 Web Shell
- step: Found a file of unencrypted usernames and passwords
  tactic: Credential Access
  technique: T1552.001 Credentials In Files
- step: Ran about 9,000 queries on 48 databases
  tactic: Collection
  technique: T1213 Data from Information Repositories
- step: Compressed and split the stolen files, then downloaded them
  tactic: Collection, then Exfiltration
  technique: T1560 Archive Collected Data (per the DOJ indictment)
blocks.caption: The Equifax intrusion in ATT&CK terms, written as YAML (a plain-text data format). The technique names are ATT&CK's own; the mapping is our reading of the report.

blocks.md: Why bother mapping? Because each technique comes with documented detections and mitigations, so a mapping becomes a checklist. For Equifax: patch and scan internet-facing applications (T1190), alert on new script files appearing in web directories (T1505.003), keep credentials in a secrets manager instead of files (T1552.001), alert on unusual query volume (T1213), and watch outbound traffic. Security teams describe threat groups the same way: ATT&CK's entry for WannaCry lists techniques such as Windows Service creation, Remote System Discovery, Exploitation of Remote Services and Data Encrypted for Impact, matching what CISA saw in lesson 7.

blocks.prompt: Colonial Pipeline's attacker logged in through a legacy VPN account with valid credentials. Which ATT&CK tactic is that step, and why is it hard to detect?
blocks.reveal: It is **Initial Access**, through techniques such as T1133 External Remote Services and T1078 Valid Accounts. It is hard to detect because nothing is exploited: the VPN sees a correct username and password, which looks like an employee logging in. Detection has to rely on context: an account that has not been used for months, a new location or device, or a login at an odd hour. ATT&CK lists Valid Accounts under several tactics at once (it also gives persistence and privilege), which is part of why stolen passwords are so valuable.

blocks.md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.
Kill chain: seven phases, and breaking any link stops the intrusion. ATT&CK: tactics (why) and techniques (how) with IDs, the shared language of detection rules and threat reports.

blocks.question: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
options: A tactic is the attacker's goal at that step; a technique is a specific way of achieving it
Tactics are for Windows, techniques for Linux
Tactics are legal, techniques are illegal
There is no difference; they are synonyms
blocks.explain: MITRE describes tactics as the why (for example Credential Access) and techniques as the how (for example T1552.001 Credentials In Files). One tactic has many techniques.

blocks.question: Why do defenders like the kill chain's idea that 'one mitigation breaks the chain'?
options: It means only the first phase needs defending
It means attacks are impossible
It means a detection or block at any later phase can still stop the intrusion before its objective
It means attackers must use malware
blocks.explain: Every phase is a chance to stop the attacker, so defences deep inside the network (like Equifax's traffic monitor, had it worked) still matter even after the initial break-in.

lessons.title: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent

blocks.md:
No single control is perfect. Patches arrive late, people click links, monitoring breaks. **Defence in depth** is the response: stack several different barriers so an attacker who beats one still meets the next. NIST's glossary describes it as a strategy that combines people, technology and operations to put barriers across multiple layers of an organisation.

Tiny example: a bank vault has a locked front door, guards, cameras, a vault door, a time lock and insurance. A thief must beat all of them; the bank needs only one to work.

It helps to sort layers by *when* they act. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, published in February 2024, organises all security outcomes into six functions:

- **Govern**: strategy, roles, policy and oversight of the rest.
- **Identify**: understand your assets and risks (Equifax's missing inventory lived here).
- **Protect**: safeguards such as access control, training, data security, patching.
- **Detect**: find attacks and anomalies (Equifax's blind traffic monitor).
- **Respond**: contain and handle an incident (Colonial's shutdown).
- **Recover**: restore normal operations (backups, rebuilds).

A design with only Protect layers fails silently the day one of them breaks.

Why do layers help so much, and when do they stop helping? Use a simple model. Suppose each layer independently stops a fraction $s$ of attacks. An attack must get past all $n$ layers, so the chance it succeeds is $(1-s)^n$. Now add one realistic complication: with probability $q$, a shared weakness disables every layer at once (one stolen administrator password that unlocks every system, say). Then the pass rate is $q + (1-q)(1-s)^n$.

blocks.title: Attack success rate versus number of layers (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Layers that each stop half of attacks: one layer lets 50% through, three let 12.5% through. Independent layers multiply.
Good layers (s = 0.9): three of them let through 0.1%, one attack in a thousand. This is the promise of defence in depth.
Add a 10% chance that one shared weakness disables everything: three layers now let through about 10.1%, and six layers barely help. The floor is q.
Simplified: real layers are never fully independent and attackers adapt. The lesson holds anyway: remove shared failure points before adding more layers.

blocks.code:
# Chance that an attack gets through every layer, under a simple model:
# each layer independently stops a fraction s of attacks, and with
# probability q a shared weakness switches all layers off at once.
def pass_rate(s, n, q=0.0):
    return q + (1 - q) * (1 - s) ** n

print(round(pass_rate(0.5, 1), 4))         # one mediocre layer: 0.5
print(round(pass_rate(0.9, 3), 4))         # three good layers: 0.001
print(round(pass_rate(0.9, 3, q=0.1), 4))  # plus a shared flaw: 0.1009
print(round(pass_rate(0.9, 6, q=0.1), 4))  # doubling the layers: 0.1
blocks.caption: The same model in Python, with the numbers from the figure.

blocks.md:
Real shared failures look like this: the same password on every server; one administrator account that can reach backups *and* production (ransomware deletes both); a monitoring device that dies without telling anyone (Equifax); every layer bought from one vendor with one bug.

Now replay **Colonial Pipeline** as a layered design. Identify: an inventory of remote-access accounts would have flagged a legacy VPN profile nobody should use. Protect: disabling it removes the door; requiring a second factor at login would mean a password alone was not enough. Detect: an alert on a dormant account logging in. Respond: Colonial did isolate OT quickly. Recover: CISA's DarkSide advisory stresses offline backups for both IT and OT networks, because ransomware cannot encrypt what it cannot reach.

blocks.title: Layers between a stolen password and the pipeline

scenes.caption: A hypothetical layered design for the Colonial scenario. Each layer works differently, so one trick rarely beats them all.
Testimony says the profile existed and the attacker had working credentials: the first two layers were missing or did not apply.
Response that did work: staff stopped the pipeline within about 70 minutes of finding the note to protect OT. A Detect layer would have bought that hour earlier, before encryption.

blocks.md: Defence in depth means several *different* layers across Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, so that one failure does not mean total failure. The math only works when layers fail independently: hunt down shared passwords, shared admin accounts and silent monitoring first.

blocks.question: Three layers each stop 90% of attacks, independently. What fraction of attacks get through all three?
blocks.explain: Each layer lets 10% through, and independence means the fractions multiply: 0.1 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.001, which is 0.1%.

blocks.question: A company has firewall, antivirus and monitoring, but all three are managed with one administrator password that is also used for email. What is the main weakness?
options: Too few layers
A shared failure point: one stolen password disables every layer
Antivirus is obsolete
Firewalls slow the network
blocks.explain: In the model, the shared password is q: if it is stolen, all layers fail together and adding more layers does not lower the floor. Separate, strongly protected admin credentials restore independence.

lessons.title: Who does security work: the job families

blocks.md: Security is not one job. NIST's [NICE](https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/about) Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NICE was once short for National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education; the program now goes only by the acronym) exists to give the field a common language for its many kinds of work. For a beginner, five families cover most roles. Each lines up with parts of the CSF functions from the last lesson.

- **Offence (offensive security)**: penetration testers and red teams attack systems *with permission* to find weaknesses first. NIST defines a **red team** as a group authorised to emulate a potential adversary's attack against an organisation, to show the impact of real attacks and what works for the defenders, the **blue team**. Vulnerability researchers, who find new bugs and report them (lesson 5), sit nearby.
- **Defence (security operations)**: SOC analysts (SOC: security operations centre) triage alerts, detection engineers write the rules that create alerts, incident responders contain and clean up attacks, threat intelligence analysts track who is attacking whom.
- **Application security (AppSec)**: engineers who make software secure while it is built, through design review, code review, testing tools and fixing bug classes.
- **Cloud security**: engineers who secure cloud accounts, identity and permissions, and configuration.
- **GRC (governance, risk and compliance)**: people who run risk assessments (lesson 2's table), policies, audits and frameworks such as the CSF.

blocks.title: Job families and the CSF functions they mostly serve

scenes.caption: A rough map, not a rulebook: every family touches several functions. It shows where each family spends most of its time.
Offence feeds Identify: a pentest or red team exercise finds the weaknesses and the paths through them before a real attacker does, and reports them.
AppSec and cloud security build Protect: secure code, safe defaults, least-privilege permissions. Their work prevents whole classes of bugs.
SOC, detection and incident response own Detect, Respond and Recover: noticing the attack, containing it, and restoring service.
GRC owns Govern: deciding which risks matter, who is responsible, and proving controls actually work. In the Equifax report, missing governance of patching was a core finding.

blocks.md: What do these jobs have in common? Reading code and logs, writing small scripts to automate checks, and explaining risk to people who are not security specialists. A typical first task in a SOC is answering a simple question from logs. On Linux servers, the SSH login service (sshd; SSH means Secure Shell) records failed logins, and a short pipeline of standard tools answers "who is guessing passwords here?".

blocks.title: Counting failed SSH logins by source address
blocks.code:
# A first-day SOC task: who is guessing SSH passwords on this server?
# Sample lines from /var/log/auth.log (Debian and Ubuntu):
#   sshd[811]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
#   sshd[811]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2
#   sshd[930]: Accepted publickey for ana from 198.51.100.4 port 51200 ssh2
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log |
  grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" |
  awk '{print $2}' |
  sort | uniq -c | sort -rn |
  head -5

scenes.caption: Two failed attempts and one success. The IP addresses are from ranges reserved for documentation, so they are safe to use in examples.

scenes.output:
...Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
...Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2
scenes.caption: grep keeps only the failed attempts. Successful logins are dropped.
grep -o prints only the matching part. Matching on 'from' plus an address works whether or not the line says 'invalid user'.
awk prints the second word: the address alone.
sort groups identical lines, uniq -c counts them, sort -rn puts the biggest count first, head keeps the top five. On a real internet server this list is usually long.

blocks.md: What the analyst does next is the real skill: are these guesses for accounts that exist? Did any address later succeed? Is password login even needed, or can the server accept keys only? Answering those questions is triage; turning the answers into a rule that alerts automatically is detection engineering.

Five families: offence, defence (SOC, detection, IR), AppSec, cloud security and GRC. They need the same foundations this track teaches: how systems work, how attacks work, and how to read, script and explain.

blocks.question: A company hires people to break into its own systems, with written permission, so the defenders can practise. What is this group called in NIST's terms?
options: A blue team
A GRC team
A red team
A CNA
blocks.explain: NIST defines a red team as a group authorised to emulate a potential adversary's attack. The blue team defends against it.

blocks.question: In the SSH pipeline, why match `from [0-9.]+` instead of taking a fixed word position with awk on the whole line?
options: Because lines for nonexistent users contain two extra words ('invalid user'), so the address is not always in the same position
Because grep is faster than awk
Because awk cannot read log files
Because IP addresses are encrypted in the log
blocks.explain: The 'invalid user' variant shifts every later field by two. Matching the text right after 'from' finds the address in both formats.

lessons.title: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure

blocks.md:
Everything in this track can be used to protect or to harm. The difference, legally and ethically, is **authorisation**: permission from the owner of the system. Testing a system you own, or one whose owner has given you written permission, is security work. The same actions without permission can be a crime, even if you mean well and even if you change nothing.

Tiny example: you notice your gym's member website shows your account at a web address ending in `id=1001`. Changing it to `1002` to "see if it is vulnerable" means deliberately looking at someone else's data. Do not. Report what you noticed instead.

**United States: the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)**, 18 U.S.C. 1030. Among other offences, it covers anyone who intentionally accesses a computer *without authorization* or *exceeds authorized access* and thereby obtains information. Its 1986 amendments added the provision under which Robert Morris was later convicted, and the appeals court held that releasing the worm counted as access without authorisation even though Morris said the aim was to show security weaknesses.

In 2021 the US Supreme Court narrowed "exceeds authorized access" in [*Van Buren v. United States*](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/19-783_k53l.pdf): a person exceeds authorised access when they enter parts of a computer, such as files, folders or databases, that are off-limits to them, not merely when they misuse data they were allowed to see. Accessing someone else's records by changing an ID is the off-limits kind.

**United Kingdom: the [Computer Misuse Act 1990](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1990/18/contents)**. Section 1 makes it an offence to make a computer perform any function intending to access a program or data when you know the access is unauthorised. Section 2 covers doing so to commit further crimes, section 3 covers unauthorised acts that impair a computer's operation, and section 3ZA covers acts causing serious damage. Section 3A covers making, supplying or obtaining any "article" (which includes programs and data) intending it to be used for an offence under section 1, 3 or 3ZA, or supplying one believing it is likely to be. That is why the *intent* and *context* around security tools matter.

Other countries have similar laws. This lesson is orientation, not legal advice.

Rules of thumb that keep you on the right side: test only systems you own or have written permission to test; stay inside the agreed scope (systems, dates, methods); stop and report the moment you see other people's data; never keep or share it. A bug bounty programme's published rules are a form of written permission, but only for what they list.

When you do find a problem, use **coordinated disclosure** (lesson 5): tell the owner privately, give them time to fix it, and publish only afterwards. To make that easy, organisations publish a **security.txt** file, defined in RFC 9116, at a fixed address on their website. Two fields are required: `Contact`, how to report a vulnerability, and `Expires`, a date after which the file is stale (the RFC recommends less than a year ahead). Optional fields include a link to the disclosure `Policy` that says what researchers may and may not do.

blocks.code:
# Served at https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt  (RFC 9116)
Contact: mailto:security@example.com
Expires: 2027-06-30T00:00:00Z
Policy: https://example.com/vulnerability-disclosure-policy
Preferred-Languages: en
blocks.caption: A minimal security.txt. Before reporting, a researcher reads it; before publishing one, a company makes sure someone actually reads that mailbox.

blocks.title: Doing it right: from finding to fix

scenes.caption: You notice something odd while using the service normally. You stop there and do not probe further without permission.
You look up the contact and policy. If there is a bug bounty or disclosure policy, its scope tells you what testing, if any, is allowed.
You report privately with enough detail to reproduce it, and without other users' data.
They fix it and protect users, then everyone can talk about it. If a vendor ignores you, coordinators such as CISA's CVD program can help.

blocks.prompt: A friend runs a small online shop and says over chat: 'Sure, test my site.' Is that enough before you start scanning it?
blocks.reveal: **Get it in writing, with a scope.** A chat message is better than nothing, but a short written agreement should say which systems (your friend may not own the hosting platform or payment provider, and cannot authorise testing of those), which dates, which methods, and who to call if something breaks. Professional penetration tests always start with this, usually called rules of engagement. If the site runs on a third-party platform, that platform's own policy also applies.

blocks.md:
**Where to practise legally.** These platforms exist so you can attack things on purpose, with permission built in:

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security): free web-security labs.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): a deliberately insecure web shop you run yourself.
- [picoCTF](https://picoctf.org/): beginner capture-the-flag puzzles across all topics.
- [OverTheWire](https://overthewire.org/wargames/): Linux and security wargames; start with Bandit.
- [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/): structured systems and exploitation practice.
- [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) and [Hack The Box](https://www.hackthebox.com/): guided rooms and labs, many free.
- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): defensive investigations from logs and evidence.
Authorisation is the line. Own it or get written, scoped permission; stop at other people's data; report privately and give owners time to fix. Practise on platforms built for it.

blocks.question: Under the Supreme Court's reading in Van Buren, which act most clearly 'exceeds authorized access'?
options: An employee reads a report they are allowed to read, for a personal reason
A user forgets to log out
A researcher reads a public security.txt file
A logged-in user changes an ID in a URL to open another customer's records that are off-limits to them
blocks.explain: The Court tied 'exceeds authorized access' to entering areas of a computer, such as files or databases, that are off-limits to you. Reading another customer's records fits; misusing data you may see is the case the Court excluded.

blocks.question: Which two security.txt fields does RFC 9116 require?
options: Policy and Hiring
Contact and Expires
Encryption and Canonical
Preferred-Languages and Policy
blocks.explain: RFC 9116 says Contact must always be present and Expires must always be present (exactly once). The others are optional.
